wine.name: South Block Reserve Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from the founder's ungrafted vines.
wine.sites: The South Block, ten rows in a corner of the original Eyrie Vineyard in the Dundee Hills, first planted in 1968 where six soil types meet; the vines grow on their own roots without irrigation.
wine.making: Made as the house makes all its Pinot Noir: fermented by native yeasts, mostly destemmed with at most a small share of whole clusters, and aged in old oak barrels, barely one in twenty five of them new. Malolactic fermentation comes naturally and in full; the wine is racked little, never fined and only lightly filtered.
wine.glass: Pale ruby in the glass: sour cherry, wild strawberry and rose petal, then fennel, leather and damp earth; light in body and alcohol, its acidity bright and its tannin fine and gentle.
wine.ageing: Delicate and perfumed young, it gains savoury depth over twenty years and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, a little cool to keep its perfume; decant only an old bottle, gently off its sediment; a wide Burgundy glass.

label.means: Ten rows of the original Eyrie Vineyard, bottled apart since the 1975 vintage.
An AVA within the Willamette Valley, in force since 2005, so older vintages could not carry it.
Oregon asks at least 90 per cent of Pinot Noir to use its name, where federal law asks 75.

records.table: The Eyrie Vineyards' South Block Reserve comes from ten rows planted in 1968, in a corner of the original Dundee Hills vineyard; the house is credited with the Willamette Valley's first Pinot Noir. Pale, with sour cherry, rose and damp earth, its 1975 carried Oregon's name to Paris and Beaune.
records.story: David Lett (1939 to 2008) studied viticulture at the University of California at Davis and came north to plant Pinot Noir against the advice of his professors. In 1965 he brought some three thousand cuttings to the Willamette Valley, set them out in a nursery and then moved them to a former orchard in the Dundee Hills that he bought in 1966. The farm took the name The Eyrie from the red-tailed hawks nesting in its firs. Lett is credited with the valley's first Pinot Noir and the first Pinot Gris in the United States, and he made his first vintage in 1970. The South Block, ten rows planted in 1968, was first bottled on its own in 1975. In 1979 that wine was poured blind among Pinot Noirs at a tasting in Paris held by the guide Gault-Millau, and it finished ahead of several red Burgundies. A year later the Beaune house of Joseph Drouhin restaged the tasting at home, and the Oregon wine came second, narrowly, to a Drouhin Chambolle-Musigny of 1959. Burgundy took notice, and in 1987 the Drouhin family made its own purchase in the Dundee Hills. After Lett's death in 2008 his son set the South Block bottling aside for some years in tribute, then revived it. To open one is to taste the Willamette Valley's Pinot Noir at its source.

others.name: Original Vines Pinot Noir
others.note: From the vines of the first plantings, the house's statement of its own history.

others.name: Estate Pinot Gris
others.note: From the grape Lett is credited with planting first in the United States, in the 1960s.

traps: The South Block was planted in 1968, after the founder's first vines of 1965; it is a corner of the original vineyard, not its first planting.
The 1975 South Block shone at Gault-Millau's tasting in Paris in 1979 and came second at the Beaune rematch of 1980; neither was the Judgement of Paris of 1976.
Its pale colour and light body are the house's chosen style, not a sign of a weak year or of a tired bottle.

cards.front: The Eyrie's South Block Reserve: when were its vines planted, and when was it first bottled apart?
cards.back: Planted in 1968 in a corner of the original Dundee Hills vineyard; bottled on its own from the 1975 vintage.

cards.front: Which Oregon wine came second to a 1959 Drouhin Chambolle-Musigny at a rematch in Beaune in 1980?
cards.back: The Eyrie Vineyards' 1975 South Block Reserve Pinot Noir, a result that drew the Drouhin family to Oregon.

questions.q: Which description fits the way The Eyrie makes its South Block Reserve Pinot Noir?
opts: Native yeasts and old barrels, barely any of them new
Cultured yeasts and new French oak throughout
Whole bunches for most of the fermentation
Long ageing in large American oak casks
questions.exp: The house ferments its reds with native yeasts and buys barely one new barrel in twenty five; whole clusters are at most a small share, and the barrels are old, not new.

questions.q: In 1980 a Beaune house restaged a Paris tasting, and The Eyrie's 1975 South Block Reserve came second. What did the result lead to?
opts: The Drouhin family bought land in the Dundee Hills
Lett planted his first vines in the Dundee Hills
The Eyrie made its first vintage of Pinot Noir
The South Block was first bottled on its own
questions.exp: The result drew the Drouhin family of Beaune to Oregon, where it bought Dundee Hills land in 1987; the first vintage of 1970 and the first South Block bottling of 1975 came before the tasting.

report: The house's own pages date the South Block's first planting to 1968 and its first bottling as a single block to 1975, so the library's wine note for it (From the original 1965 planting) is wrong for this block, and the plan's why (Dundee Hills vines of 1966) fits the estate rather than the block.

founded keeps the library's 1966; Wikipedia gives 1965, the year the vines reached the valley and went into a nursery, and the house dates its first vines to February 1965, so the library's holdings line (set in 1965) runs the nursery into the Dundee Hills planting.

The 1979 placing is told variously (top ten, top three, a triumph), so the story says only that the wine finished ahead of several red Burgundies; the margin at Beaune in 1980 (two tenths of a point) rests on one source and is left out.

The making line is the house's general method for its Pinot Noir, read from its winemaking page; no South Block sheet giving months in barrel could be read, and eyrievineyards.com refused the one fetch, so its pages were read through search summaries.
The year the South Block bottling returned after 2008 is 2013 on some of the house's pages and 2015 on another, so the story says only that it was revived.

say is empty: no source settled how the house says Eyrie (Jancis Robinson reports that Lett chose a name nobody could spell or pronounce), and the winery building's past as a turkey processing plant was found in no source and is left out.

The purchase of the Dundee Hills land in 1966 rests on Wikipedia's page on David Lett and the library's founding year; Lett's dates rest on the house's memorial biography (1939 to 2008) and Wikipedia.
Living people kept out: the founder's wife, who named the estate, and his son.

changed: say: empty becomes EYE-ree, as a regional tourism body (Visit McMinnville) and Oregon Business give the house's name; the house's own pages give the hawks' nest behind it.

wine.ageing: the 1970 and the 1975 were alive decades after their vintages is cut; the 1970 found alive at the house's tasting of 2008 was its Pinot Noir from before the South Block was bottled apart, so not this wine, and the 1975's later showing rests on Decanter alone. The window of twenty years and more stays, said of a strong vintage.
wine.label[1]: approved in 2005 becomes in force since 2005; TTB published the final rule on 30 November 2004 and it took effect on 31 January 2005, by TTB's press release and the Federal Register.

wine.label[2]: at least 90 per cent of the named grape becomes of Pinot Noir; Oregon lets eighteen varieties follow the federal 75, by the Oregon Wine Board and the Willamette Valley Wineries Association.
story: some three thousand young vines becomes cuttings; the house's pages and two secondary accounts have cuttings rooted in a nursery near Corvallis from February 1965.
story: His wife named the farm becomes The farm took the name The Eyrie from the hawks; one account gives the naming to the founder's wife and another to the couple, so neither is kept.
open: The year the South Block bottling came back after the founder's last vintage of 2007: 2013 on the house's sheets of 2017 and 2019, after a gap of five or six years by merchants; the story says only that it was revived.
The placing of 1979 is told as top ten, third among the Pinot Noirs or a win; the story keeps ahead of several red Burgundies, which every account allows.

wine.name: Pinot Noir Laurène
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, all of it grown on the family's own estate.
wine.sites: The family's estate in the Dundee Hills, on the red volcanic Jory soil of those hills; Laurène draws on chosen barrels from across the estate rather than one block.
wine.making: Picked by hand into small boxes, sorted, destemmed and fermented with indigenous yeasts over seven to twelve days of punching down and pumping over, in a four level winery that moves the wine by gravity. After twelve to fourteen months in French oak, a share of it new, the winemaker chooses the barrels with extra complexity, length and depth for Laurène, and the blend rests before bottling.
wine.glass: Dark and red cherry, dried rose petal and clove over a touch of toast and candied orange peel; silky in texture, held by a firm frame and velvety tannin.
wine.ageing: By the house's own guide it is at its fullest after ten to twelve years and keeps for about fifteen; younger, it rewards air.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; half an hour in a decanter for a young bottle, a slow pour off the sediment for an old one; a broad bowled Burgundy glass.

label.means: Named for the eldest daughter of the family's winemaker; first made from the 1992 vintage.
The Oregon estate of the Drouhin family of Beaune, founded in 1987.
Hills known for red volcanic Jory soil; a sub-appellation of the Willamette Valley in force since 2005.

records.table: Burgundy came to the Dundee Hills with Domaine Drouhin Oregon, the Beaune family's estate, and Laurène, named for the winemaker's eldest daughter, is its pick of the cellar's barrels. Its cherry, rose and clove, silky but firmly framed, bring Burgundian restraint to Oregon's red soil.
records.story: The Drouhin family's road to Oregon ran through two tastings. At a large blind tasting of wines from many countries, held in Paris in 1979 by the Gault-Millau guide, The Eyrie Vineyards' 1975 South Block Reserve placed above several red Burgundies among the Pinot Noirs. In 1980 the head of the Drouhin house restaged the contest in Beaune, and this time the Oregon wine took second place, a fraction behind the house's own Chambolle-Musigny of 1959. The result stayed with the family. In 1987 it bought land in the Dundee Hills, and the head of the house named his daughter, of the fourth generation, winemaker from the start. The first vintage followed in 1988, and in 1989 the family built a winery on four levels so that grapes and wine could move by gravity rather than by pump. In 1992 the winemaker gave her eldest daughter's name to a new selection of the cellar's chosen barrels, and Laurène is the wine the house holds up as its flagship. Other cuvées carry the names of members of the family, Louise for a further Pinot Noir and Arthur for Chardonnay, and the family added a second estate, Roserock, in the Eola-Amity Hills. Laurène answers a question guests often put: what Burgundy's own hands make of Dundee Hills fruit.

others.name: Dundee Hills Pinot Noir
others.note: The estate's main Pinot Noir, the first wine the family made in Oregon, in 1988.

others.name: Cuvée Louise

traps: Do not credit the Judgement of Paris of 1976 with drawing the Drouhin family to Oregon: The Eyrie's showings of 1979 and 1980 did.
Laurène is a selection of barrels from across the Dundee Hills estate, not a single vineyard; the cuvées carry family names.
Roserock, the family's second Oregon estate, is in the Eola-Amity Hills, not the Dundee Hills.

cards.front: Domaine Drouhin Oregon's Laurène: how are its barrels chosen?
cards.back: After twelve to fourteen months in French oak, the winemaker picks the barrels of estate Pinot Noir with extra complexity, length and depth.

cards.back: 1987, after The Eyrie's 1975 Pinot Noir ran a Drouhin Chambolle-Musigny close at Beaune in 1980.

opts: It gathers the cellar's chosen barrels of estate fruit
It comes from the Roserock estate in Eola-Amity
It is aged for two years in American oak
It is fermented as whole bunches alone
questions.exp: Laurène is made from barrels the winemaker selects for complexity, length and depth, all from the Dundee Hills estate; Roserock lies in the Eola-Amity Hills and gives wines of its own name.

questions.q: Domaine Drouhin Oregon bought its Dundee Hills land in 1987. In which year was Laurène first made?
questions.exp: Laurène was first made in 1992; 1988 was the estate's first vintage, 1989 the year its gravity winery was built, and 1980 the year of the Beaune rematch.

report: The house's Our Estate page prints Est. 1989 beside a founding in 1987; 1989 is the year the winery was built (a construction photograph of 1989 on the house's own pages), so founded keeps the library's 1987.

The share of new oak (a fifth) and the twelve to fourteen months are given by the house for its estate Pinot Noir in general, with Laurène chosen from those barrels, so the making says a share of it new.

Left out for want of a second source: the year the estate's own grapes were first used (1990, Decanter alone), the head of the house's first visit to Oregon (1961, one Decanter page), the density of planting, and a claim that the house was the first from Burgundy in Oregon.

Living people kept out: the head of the house who bought the land and staged the 1980 tasting, his daughter the winemaker, her children, and the Oregon grower who pointed him to the site; the library's why names the first two.
The library's style line (red cherry and iron, whole cluster used with discipline) was not found in the house's notes, which say destemmed; the glass follows the house's own notes.

changed: wine.sites: red volcanic Jory soil and the shallower Nekia becomes the red volcanic Jory soil of those hills; the house's pages say volcanic and name no series, Jory stands on the library's style line and the region's summary, and Nekia was found in no source of this check.
wine.label[0], table and story: the elder daughter becomes the eldest daughter, the house's own word in its letters on Laurène, which also date the first vintage, 1992, to the year of her birth.

story: a blind tasting of Pinot Noirs becomes a large blind tasting of wines from many countries, among whose Pinot Noirs the Eyrie wine finished; the Olympiades of 1979 tasted some 330 wines from 33 countries by three accounts.
open: That the founder's daughter was winemaker from the first vintage of 1988 rests on the library's why and the house's pages; it was not searched again.

wine.name: Evenstad Reserve Pinot Noir
wine.sites: A selection of barrels made each year and labelled Willamette Valley rather than one hill. The house's first vineyard, the Mark Bradford, planted in 1993 in the Dundee Hills and named for the founders' son, began estates that later reached into the Eola-Amity Hills and Yamhill-Carlton.
wine.making: Each year the cellar sets aside the barrels it chooses for the reserve, a habit of the house since its first vintage. The wine is aged for well over a year in French oak barrels, a good part of them new, and since 2001 it has been made in a winery built on five levels, so that the wine falls from stage to stage by gravity.
wine.glass: Black cherry, bramble and cola, lifted by lilac over sassafras and clove; generous for Oregon Pinot Noir, with ripe, velvety tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Generous from the outset; it goes on gaining in the cellar for a decade and more when the year is strong.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for half an hour; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The founding family's name, on the reserve selection of barrels the house has made since its first vintage, 1990.
The valley's AVA of 1983, wider than the Dundee Hills where the house stands.

records.table: The Evenstad Reserve bears the name of the family who founded Domaine Serene in the Dundee Hills in 1989, and it has drawn on barrels set apart each year since the first vintage, 1990. Here the valley shows its riper, richer side: black cherry, cola and clove, full and velvety.
records.story: Domaine Serene began on a hilltop in the Dundee Hills. Ken Evenstad (1943 to 2020), who ran the pharmaceutical company Upsher-Smith Laboratories, founded the estate there with his wife in 1989 and named it for their daughter. Their first Pinot Noir followed in 1990, and the barrels they set apart that year made the house's first Reserve, the start of the Evenstad Reserve, which the house calls its flagship. In 1993 they planted their first vineyard, the Mark Bradford, named for their son, and in 1994 they turned a historic building of 1913 in the town of Carlton into their first winery. In 2001 the house moved into a winery of its own on the hill, a building on five levels in which the wine moves by gravity. The house also makes Chardonnay, with an Evenstad Reserve of its own. In 2015 the family bought Château de la Crée in Burgundy's Côte d'Or, taking the house to Burgundy itself. Ken Evenstad died in 2020. Next to the pale Pinot Noir of the valley's first growers, the Evenstad Reserve shows the region's riper, fuller side.

others.name: Evenstad Reserve Chardonnay
others.note: The Chardonnay of the same name, labelled Dundee Hills.

others.name: Yamhill Cuvée Pinot Noir

traps: Evenstad Reserve is labelled Willamette Valley, not Dundee Hills, though the house and its first vineyard stand in the Dundee Hills.
Domaine Serene is an Oregon house founded by an American family in 1989, not a Burgundy domaine; its Burgundy estate, Château de la Crée, came in 2015.
Mark Bradford names a vineyard; the Evenstad Reserve is chosen barrel by barrel, not drawn from one site.

cards.front: What did Domaine Serene finish building in the Dundee Hills in 2001?

questions.q: A guest reads Willamette Valley, not Dundee Hills, on Domaine Serene's Evenstad Reserve. What does that tell the guest?
opts: It claims the valley's wider AVA rather than one hill
It is a single vineyard wine from Carlton
It is a blend of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay
It was made in the family's Burgundy cellar
questions.exp: Willamette Valley is the wider AVA of 1983 that holds the Dundee Hills; the wine is Pinot Noir alone, made in Oregon, and Carlton was only the site of the first winery.

questions.q: Which Burgundy property did the family behind Domaine Serene buy in 2015?
opts: Château de la Crée in the Côte d'Or
The négociant house of Joseph Drouhin
A cellar of barrels in the town of Beaune
A Grand Cru parcel in Chablis
questions.exp: In 2015 the founding family bought Château de la Crée in Burgundy's Côte d'Or; Joseph Drouhin is the Beaune family behind Domaine Drouhin Oregon, and the house bought neither a Beaune cellar nor a Chablis parcel.

report: Not in the library: the founding in 1989, the first vintage of 1990, the Mark Bradford planting of 1993, the Carlton winery of 1994, the gravity winery of 2001 and Château de la Crée in 2015 rest on the house's own timeline and About page, with 1989 and 1990 also in a merchant's account and 2015 in a biography published by a wine festival.

Ken Evenstad's dates (1943 to 2020) rest on the Oregon Wine Press and the Drinks Business; obituaries call him the founder of Upsher-Smith Laboratories, a company older than his part in it, so the story says he ran it.
The oak line rests on the house's figures for the 2014 and 2015 vintages (sixteen and seventeen months, about three fifths new), so it says well over a year and a good part new, with no figure.

The first vintages of 1990 to about 1995 must have come from bought grapes, since the first estate vineyard was planted in 1993, and the label is Willamette Valley, so the sites line does not claim the wine comes only from the Dundee Hills.
Château de la Crée is placed in Santenay by one source and in the Côte d'Or by the house, so the record names only the Côte d'Or.
Living people kept out: the founder's wife, who leads the house, their daughter and son, and every winemaker; the vineyard and the house keep the names they were given.

wine.glass: blackberry becomes bramble and full in body becomes generous; the house's note for 2022 gives dark black cherry, sassafras, cola, lilac and bramble, and its note for 2021 a light body, so a full body is not the wine's constant.

wine.label[0]: the family's name given to the selection since 1990 becomes the reserve selection made since 1990; the house's timeline calls the first release the 1990 Reserve and no source shows the family's name on the label from the start.
table: has been its flagship since the first vintage of 1990 becomes its line of chosen barrels runs back to the first vintage, 1990, for the same reason.
story: freshly logged land high in the Dundee Hills becomes a hilltop site, the house's own words; nothing of logging was found.
story: the barrels set apart in 1990 became the Evenstad Reserve becomes made the house's first Reserve, the start of the Evenstad Reserve.
story: the plans of 1999 for the hill winery are cut, found in no source of this check; the winery on five levels finished in 2001 stays, on the house's timeline.

sources: Wine.com's page for the 2015 gives way to Drug Store News's obituary, which gives Ken Evenstad's birth in 1943, the founding with his wife in 1989 and the daughter whose name the estate carries.
open: The grapes of the first vintages, before the Mark Bradford vineyard bore fruit, were not traced; the record does not say where the 1990 fruit grew.
Ken Evenstad bought Upsher-Smith in 1968 or 1969 by different obituaries; the story says only that he ran it.

wine.name: Argyle Extended Tirage Brut
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, Pinot Noir usually the larger part and the share changing with each vintage, with a little Meunier in some later years.
wine.sites: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from vineyards across the Willamette Valley; a sister bottling, Extended Tirage Knudsen Vineyard Brut, comes from the Dundee Hills vineyard planted in the early 1970s that has given Argyle fruit since 1987.
wine.making: Traditional method throughout: the base wines are fermented mostly in stainless steel, with a small share in neutral barrels. After the second fermentation in bottle the wine rests about ten years on its yeast in the house's cellar, and it is disgorged on demand with a low dosage of a few grams a litre.
wine.glass: Brioche, roasted hazelnut and honeycomb over baked apple, nectarine and orange peel, with a fine, persistent mousse and a dry, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Released ready to drink after about ten years on its yeast; disgorged on demand so that it reaches the glass fresh, it needs no further cellaring.
wine.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a tulip or a white wine glass rather than a narrow flute.

label.means: Aged on its yeast in bottle for about ten years before disgorging.
Dry: the term Champagne uses for less than twelve grams of sugar a litre; here only a few.
A blend of sites from across the whole valley rather than one vineyard.

records.table: Founded in the town of Dundee in 1987 to make traditional method sparkling wine, Argyle rests its Extended Tirage Brut, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, about ten years on its yeast before disgorging. Expect brioche and roasted hazelnut over baked apple, with a fine, dry finish.
records.story: The belief that the cool Willamette Valley suited sparkling wine made by the traditional method of Champagne lay behind Argyle's founding in 1987, and sparkling wine has been its signature from its first year. Its first winery was a former hazelnut drying plant in the town of Dundee, which the house calls the Nuthouse, and its first bottles were riddled on those premises. From the start it drew fruit from the Knudsen Vineyard in the Dundee Hills, planted in the early 1970s, one of the older vineyards of the valley. The house also kept bottles back from its first vintage to age on their yeast, and its tirage library, the house says, keeps sparkling wines on their lees from vintages reaching back to 1987. Out of that patience came the Extended Tirage wines, held about ten years before they are disgorged, one a blend of the valley and one from the Knudsen Vineyard alone. The house makes still Pinot Noir and Chardonnay as well. For the harvest of 2014, as production grew, it moved its winemaking to nearby Newberg, and the Dundee site was kept for receiving guests. The Extended Tirage Brut shows how far Oregon has taken the method: ten years on its yeast is more than three times the thirty six months from tirage to release that Champagne asks of a vintage wine.

others.name: Vintage Brut
others.note: The vintage dated house sparkling wine of Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier.

others.name: Extended Tirage Knudsen Vineyard Brut
others.note: The same long ageing, from the Knudsen Vineyard in the Dundee Hills alone.

others.name: Julia Lee's Block Blanc de Blancs
others.note: Chardonnay from a single block of the Knudsen Vineyard.

traps: Argyle is Oregon sparkling wine made by the traditional method, not Champagne, whatever the method shares.
The Extended Tirage Brut is a Willamette Valley blend; the Extended Tirage Knudsen Vineyard Brut is the single vineyard bottling from the Dundee Hills.
Argyle's first winery, a former hazelnut drying plant, stands in the town of Dundee; the Dundee Hills is the AVA of the Knudsen Vineyard.

cards.front: Argyle Extended Tirage Brut: how long does it rest on its yeast, and when is it disgorged?
cards.back: About ten years in bottle, then disgorged on demand, so that each release reaches the glass fresh.

cards.front: What had Argyle's first winery building in the town of Dundee been before 1987?

questions.q: Where do the brioche and roasted nut notes of Argyle's Extended Tirage Brut come from?
opts: About ten years on its yeast before disgorging
Fermentation entirely in new oak barrels
A large dose of sugar at disgorging
A blend made mostly of Meunier
questions.exp: Long contact with the spent yeast in bottle gives the brioche and nutty notes; the base wines are fermented mostly in steel with a little neutral oak, and the dosage is low.

questions.q: Argyle moved its winemaking for the harvest of 2014. Where did it go?
opts: To a facility in nearby Newberg
To a cellar in the Eola-Amity Hills
To the Knudsen Vineyard in the hills
To a former hazelnut plant in Dundee
questions.exp: Production moved to Newberg for the harvest of 2014, and the house's Dundee site, where the hazelnut drying plant had been its first winery, was kept for guests; the Knudsen Vineyard gives fruit, not a cellar.

report: The library calls the first winery a former hazelnut processing plant; the house's own pages call it a former hazelnut drying facility, so the record says drying plant, and the library record and its trap should follow.
The founders are not named or described: the sources disagree on who founded the house (one winemaker alone, or with an Australian partner and the Knudsen family), and those living may not be named.
Ownership is left out: the sources give 2000 or 2001 for the sale to Australia's Petaluma group and differ on the owners since.

Two Extended Tirage wines exist, the Willamette Valley Brut of the plan and a Knudsen Vineyard Brut from the Dundee Hills; the record keeps the plan's, and its blend is told in words because the house's sheets run from a Chardonnay majority (2012) to about two thirds Pinot Noir (2015), with Meunier only from 2015.
The house's sheets for 2011 to 2013 print both three and ten years en tirage; the ten years of the house's Extended Tirage pages and the library stand.

Left out for want of a source: the year the first Extended Tirage was released; the Knudsen Vineyard's planting is 1971 or 1972 across the sources, so the record says the early 1970s, and one account has the vineyard joining Argyle in 1990, where the house says it gave fruit from 1987.

changed: table: has made traditional method sparkling wine in the town of Dundee since 1987 becomes founded in the town of Dundee in 1987; its winemaking moved to Newberg for the 2014 harvest, by the Oregon Wine Press, Pamplin Media and the house's own history.

records.place: Spring Valley, Eola-Amity Hills, Willamette Valley, Oregon

wine.name: Mt. Jefferson Cuvée Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, blended from several vineyards.
wine.sites: The house's estate vineyards in the Eola-Amity Hills, on volcanic soils, mostly Columbia River basalt, cooled by Pacific wind through the Van Duzer Corridor, long joined by fruit from neighbouring growers; from the 2024 vintage the estate alone.
wine.making: Native yeasts carry the fermentation, with roughly half of the fruit as whole bunches with their stems and the rest destemmed. The wine then spends ten or eleven months on its lees in French oak barrels, about a fifth of them new, and is bottled without fining or filtration.
wine.glass: Tart cherry, raspberry and plum over rose, black tea and a peppery, savoury lift from the stems; light to medium in body, lively in acidity, with silky tannin and a lingering finish.
wine.ageing: Lively and open early on; a good year keeps and softens for about a decade.
wine.serve: 15 to 16 degrees Celsius, on the cool side; it needs no decanter; a wide Burgundy glass.

records.table: Roughly half whole bunches and native yeasts give the Mt. Jefferson Cuvée of Cristom Vineyards, in the Eola-Amity Hills, its peppery, savoury lift over tart cherry and raspberry. A blend of vineyards, it is the house's flagship and the door to its style.
records.story: In 1992 a family bought the abandoned Pellier winery in the Spring Valley of Polk County, in the hills that would become the Eola-Amity Hills, and founded Cristom there, naming it by joining the first names of its two children. Its first vintage was made the same autumn. Of the vines on the property, the family kept one block, planted in 1982 by the earlier owners, and renamed it Marjorie after the founder's mother; it gave a wine of its own from 1994. In 1994, too, came the first Mt. Jefferson Cuvée, a blend of estate fruit and grapes from neighbouring growers, which the house names as its flagship. The founding winemaker had come from Calera in California, where he had made the wine from the vintage of 1978 to that of 1991, and he brought its habit of fermenting Pinot Noir with whole bunches and native yeasts, which became Cristom's mark. Further estate vineyards followed, each named for a woman of the family, Louise and Jessie among them. The Eola-Amity Hills, where the Van Duzer Corridor draws cold Pacific air across the slopes each afternoon, became an AVA in 2006. With the 2024 vintage the Mt. Jefferson Cuvée was made from the estate's own vines alone for the first time. It is where the house shows what whole bunches bring to Pinot Noir.

traps: The Mt. Jefferson Cuvée is a blend of vineyards; Marjorie, Louise and Jessie are the house's single vineyard wines.
The Van Duzer Corridor is both the wind gap that cools the Eola-Amity Hills and, since 2019, an AVA of its own.
Whole bunch spice is a mark of Cristom's cellar, not of the Eola-Amity Hills appellation.

questions.exp: He made Calera's wines from the vintage of 1978 to that of 1991 and came to Oregon straight from there, bringing its whole bunches and native yeasts; Ridge is known for Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel, not Pinot Noir.

report: The plan's note is settled: the house calls the Mt. Jefferson Cuvée its flagship on its own pages and release sheets, first made in 1994; the single vineyards (Marjorie, Louise, Jessie, Eileen) are its rarer wines.
The library's why names the founding winemaker, who is living; the record says only that he came from Calera, where he made wine from 1978 to 1991 by the house's account.
The house's 2024 release sheet calls 2024 the thirtieth vintage of a wine first made in 1994, which counts one short, so the record gives no count.
Marjorie's replanting is dated 2004 by the house and 2000 elsewhere, while another account says it was never replanted, so the record leaves replanting out.
The making and the share of whole bunches and new oak are the house's figures for 2021 to 2024 (43 to 52 per cent whole bunches, 16 to 22 per cent new oak, ten or eleven months), told in words.
Left out for want of a second source: the founders' son taking over in 2012, why the wine bears Mount Jefferson's name, and the founders' home state.
Living people kept out: the founders, their children and the founding winemaker.

changed: story: The first vintage, that same year, was made from bought grapes becomes The first vintage followed that same year; the house gives 1992 for the first vintage and no source of this check says where its grapes grew.

story: On the property stood one older vineyard, planted in 1982, which the family named Marjorie becomes the family kept one block of the vines on the property, planted in 1982 by the earlier owners, and renamed it Marjorie; the house says the Mirassou family planted it in 1982 and the founder renamed it, and Oregon Wine History and a second account have the Pellier winery sold in 1992 with the rest of its vines replanted from 1993.
story: made wine from 1978 to 1991 becomes made the wine from the vintage of 1978 to that of 1991; he came for the harvest of 1978 and left in 1992 after fourteen vintages, by two accounts.
others[0]: the one vineyard already on the property becomes the vineyard planted in 1982, before the family bought the property, for the same reason.

questions[1]: the distractor Domaine Dujac, which the explanation denied without a source, becomes Ridge, in the Santa Cruz Mountains, and the explanation now says he came to Oregon straight from Calera.
open: Why the wine bears Mount Jefferson's name: a merchant's copy says the peak stands due east of the winery, one source only, so it is not added.
Marjorie's replanting stays out, as the author had it: 2000 or 2004 by different accounts, never by another.
